# Which model does which work

Three tiers, split by **who can tell whether the answer is right**.

| Tier | Work | Checked by |
|---|---|---|
| **Frontier** | Specification, briefs, review, gap review, architecture, blocking verdicts, anything irreversible, any escalation | A human, eventually — so the model has to be right the first time |
| **Implementation** | Sizeable self-contained coding chunks against a written brief | Tests and gates, plus a frontier review at the boundary |
| **Cheap / mechanical** | Renames, decided changes applied across call sites, regeneration, doc and fixture moves, harvesting | The compiler, the tests, the gates — no judgment involved |

The rule behind the table: **spend model quality where a wrong answer is expensive to
detect.** A mechanical error surfaces as a red build in seconds. A wrong judgment
surfaces weeks later as an escape, or never.

## Escalation

Escalation runs one way — cheap tier reports, frontier decides — and it is **a report,
never a guess**. An agent that hits a judgment its brief did not make stops and says:
what it found, what it did so far, and the exact question. A cheap tier that guesses to
avoid stopping costs more than it ever saved, because the wrong answer arrives wearing
the same evidence format as a right one.

The orchestrator's side of that contract: an escalation is a first-class result, not a
failure to be re-delegated with a firmer prompt. If the same question escalates twice,
the brief was underspecified — fix the brief.

## Verifiers

A **blocking** verdict is a frontier decision: it stops a commit, and the cost of a
wrong block is a human's afternoon while the cost of a wrong pass is an escape. Pin
those to the frontier model. Advisory and screening judges run on the cheap tier.

Every judge keeps a **loud fallback**: if the pinned model errors or declines, the run
falls back to the fleet default and *says so in the verdict* (`_model`, `_fallback`).
That matters more than it looks — a fallback that ran on the cheap tier and looked
identical to a pinned run is a measurement that lies. When reading eval numbers, check
the fallback column before believing the model attribution.

## Earn the assignment, do not assert it

Which tier a judge belongs in is an **eval question**, not a preference: the corpus
scores each model on labelled cases, and a cheap judge that matches the frontier on a
class of work should keep that class. Assertions about model capability age badly;
the corpus does not.
